utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone else. Douglas Stringer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution with Sarah Clanton, Uros Zigic, and our Case Manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to everyone, too. I think there is a preliminary question from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes - excuse me - Mr. President. We've had a procedural question arise that I thought best to bring to the Chamber's attention now. It's the first occasion. It probably won't be the last. The Prosecution would like to use a couple items in the redirect examination that are not on the specific list of documents that went across to the Defence for this witness. The two weeks in advance list of exhibits for use in the direct examination, one of the -- both, however, I should say both of the items that we would like to use on redirect are on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. One of them is a short video-clip similar to the others the Chamber's already seen. We identified that for Defence counsel last night and indicated we would like to use it in redirect. It goes to a video that was shown to the witness about which there's been some debate whether it was a particular meeting or not, and it's possible that the other video we would like to show could shed some light on that question. We communicated that to counsel. Counsel's indicated they don't -- if I can -- if I put it correctly, counsel does not see the need to do that on redirect examination. It's our position that it is best to do it with the witness while he's here. The second item is a document that falls within the scope of another matter that was raised on the cross-examination, the demilitarisation issue of Western Slavonia. And that document is 65 ter 1664. So we would like to use 1664 and also a video-clip, 65 ter 4842.1 on redirect. However, they're not on the list of items that went across for use as during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. The Defence -- does the Defence have a position on this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence opposes to the proposal of the Prosecution to use in his redirect any documents not listed among the documents which have to be used in the course of their direct examination. We -- it is a matter of principle, and it departs, considerably departs, from the order, guidelines that the Trial Chamber adopted and ordered to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I for myself, and I don't speak for the Bench, I for myself would wonder how any party could foresee everything that comes out of cross-examination two weeks before the direct examination starts and put documents on -- about things that come out of cross-examination without -- let's say, by surprise more or less. But that's my personal -- my personal view-point. I think the best thing to do is that we come back to you with a decision after the first break. Mr. Usher, can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzakula. As usual, I remind you that you are still under oath, and we continue with your cross-examination today, and we will finish -- well, we're pretty sure that we'll finish by the end of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we discussed the return of Croatian refugees to Benkovac. I just wanted to remind you of that. Let me ask you this first: Benkovac was in the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina before the SRK was created; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are -- that is correct. Benkovac was in the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The refugees left that area before the RSK was established?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They left during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. It seems that we have a technical problem. It seems that Judge Hall's microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning. Is it enough? Should I say anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If you would say something in B/C/S and see if I get translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I only have the camera shown on my screen. I don't have the transcript before me. I keep having to look at myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat. The refugees were moved out of Benkovac and the SAO Krajina before the RSK was established?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those refugees had left Benkovac during the war while the SAO Krajina existed, before the RSK was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We talked about Mr. Zecevic, deputy prime minister and some other ministers on the government were against their return. You also said that there was this standing apology or excuse that conditions had not been created. In your view on the 2nd of March, 1992, did you believe that such preconditions existed for the return of those 15.000 refugees to Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of March, 1992, there were no preconditions for return, because the UN forces were still not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you documents 41 and 42. The first document, number 41 -- well, perhaps it's best to look at it now again so as to remind ourselves. It is dated the 9th of July, 1992, when you, Mr. Hadzic, and Mr. Fejzovic talked to Nambiar. He referred to what Mr. Hadzic said and the need to punish those who caused incidents against non-Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, but that's not what I'm interested in right now. I'm interested in the issue of refugees and their return. He said then that the problem of refugee return to Eastern Slavonia, that is to say of non-Serbs to Eastern Slavonia, is interlinked with the return of refugees to Western Slavonia. Hence, I conclude that he wanted to say that there were no conditions necessary for the refugees to return to either Eastern or Western Slavonia as well as of Croats to Western Slavonia and Serbs to Eastern Slavonia. Did you agree with what Mr. Hadzic said at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Hadzic said that, he explained it by saying that in such houses in Eastern Slavonia where there were currently refugees from Western Slavonia, that those houses were the house of -- houses of Croats and that they could not return there because their houses were used to accommodate the Serbs from Western Slavonia. That was an obstacle. At that time there was still no conditions in existence, because the peace plan was not only under its way and there were still incidents taking place. That was directly linked to the issue of return. Serbs had to go back to Western Slavonia for the Croats to go back to Eastern Slavonia. Otherwise, the Croats could not return as their houses were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why were there no conditions met for the Serbs from Eastern Slavonia to have them moved to Western Slavonia, thus freeing up houses for the Croats to return to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have explained already and I will repeat, it was because the then-government of the RSK was against the return of Serbs to Western Slavonia, and they kept saying that there were no preconditions for that, although we have actually put some such conditions in place for the Serbs to start returning. Of course it was impossible for everyone to go back at the same time, but we initiated the process while the RSK government was against that. I must say, though, that the Croatian government was not much in favour of that either. It all resulted in no conditions having been created. If there were no conditions for the Serbs to return to Western Slavonia, then of course Croats could not return to Eastern Slavonia as their houses were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, what prevented the return of Serbs to Western Slavonia was purely administrative. In other words, it was based on the decision of the RSK government and perhaps the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both governments were against that kind of return. They kept saying that there were no conditions, where, as a matter of fact, there was no political will. They were against that. And the issue of return could only be initiated in Western Slavonia first, because, as I've said already, we had been demilitarised. There was no army there, only the police, and the process could be set in motion. If that had been allowed, the whole thing would have ended differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at number 42 next. It is a report about your meeting with Nambiar. So Mr. Hadzic was absent. I think you met on the 13th of November, 1992. When you met with Mr. Nambiar, you repeated the same thing. You said that it was first necessary for the Serbs from Eastern Slavonia to return to Western Slavonia and then that the Croats be returned to Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to explain that to Mr. Nambiar. I was trying to tell him that the return should be reciprocal in order to protect the process and the refugees. If you take a closer look, it says he had the feeling that the issue of return was of great interest among his people. So there was a clear interest of Serbs to go to the villages in Western Slavonia to see them and decide for themselves whether they wanted to return. I always connected the return of Serbs from Eastern Slavonia to Western Slavonia with the return of Croats, because I knew that only such a process in parallel would be the guarantee of cohabitation, safety of both populations en route to their homes. If the -- were the process unilateral, it would not work because the other side would be left out in the cold, thus objecting to it. That is why I always connected it to returns to Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia. They were like Siamese twins, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, if you take a look at it, he says, among other things, that Mr. Nambiar is reporting you having said that they, i.e., the UN, should request Croatian authorities to create conditions for the return of those Serbs to their homes. Can you tell me what did you mean by this, that the Croatian authorities should create conditions for the return of Serbs to their homes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian authorities were responsible for the territory that they controlled, that is to say to create conditions for safety and security and that all this burning and looting should be stopped. But you see here that I'm also mentioning some major cities that Serbs have fled such as Zagreb, Zadar, Gospic, et cetera. So if guarantees are provided for the Serbs in those cities as well for them to return to Croatia, then that would give boost to Serbs' desire to return to UNPA areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, yesterday you spoke about that in October, November, and December 1991, while the Croatian armed intervention in Western Slavonia was in progress, that many villages and many houses were torched or devastated and that that was done by the Croatian Army, and I'm talking about Serb houses. Can you tell me now, when we speak about the conditions for the return of refugees to Western Slavonia, was that perhaps an impediment for their return, because practically they had no place to go back to. All their houses were ruined or burnt.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Their houses and their villages were devastated, but in nearly every one of those villages it was possible in a very short period of time to do some repairs in order to enable their return. Since I was conducting talks with the international community, they said they were ready to start all this repair work for all the people who wished to return. So there can be no reparation of houses unless people express their will to return. People lived in Western Slavonia in very difficult conditions. They lived in a variety of facilities such as in barns and stables, et cetera, and they really wished to go back to their homes. Some of them said, We shall even put plastic sheets on our houses. I just want to go back to my home; because rural people are attached to their villages. And had that been done, then the process would have been carried out as it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that these villages were overpopulated, that people were dwelling in stables and barns, if I understood you correctly. So understand such conditions, where would these people from Eastern Slavonia go back to? Is it true that at that time that was discussed both by you and Mr. Hadzic, actually there were no proper conditions for the return?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perhaps wasn't quite clear and you didn't understand me well. When I said that people were living in barns and stables, I was talking about that part of Western Slavonia that was under Serb control, which was an area that could accommodate about 20.000 people, whereas at the time there were 50.000 people. So it was overpopulated, which forced people to live in outbuildings that were not meant for habitation. But they remained there hoping that they would leave once and go back to their villages and the same would happen with the Serbs from Eastern Slavonia and their villages. I repeat that villages like Bastajic [phoen], Caralija and Bijela were in intact, and these villages were later populated by Croats. However, at that point in time, they were intact and they were empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned these villages that were later populated by the Croats, what do you mean by "later"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was sometime after 1994 or 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's only natural that in 1992 the Croatian authorities were opposed to their return.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not exonerating the Croatian authorities at all. I think that they behaved in the identical manner as the Krajina authorities. They don't -- didn't want the Serbs to return, and that's a fact. But we wanted to implement the Vance Plan and to make it binding on everyone who accepted the plan to implement it. I have no illusions when I talk about the State of Croatia, but that was our right, and I really resented the fact that the government from the territory where I was living was obstructing the return. When we agreed with the Canadian Battalion to have people returned to 15 villages, the Krajina authorities put a stop to that. I'm not saying that perhaps the Croatian authorities wouldn't cause some incidents or maybe even some killings, but this process had to start. But tell me, they were not ready to do that. I'm not exonerating either of the two authorities because they behaved in an identical manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This intervention on the part of the Krajina authorities was the purpose there of perhaps to prevent the return of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't bother to do that in order to prevent the killing of Serbs. They just wanted to stop that process, because one process would cause the other process and the return of the Croats in Eastern Slavonia, et cetera. You can rest assured that that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing regarding this issue. In your view, when were the conditions met for the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Western Slavonia is concerned, the conditions for the return of refugees existed in early September when Mr. Marrack Goulding came to Okucani and he congratulated us on the implementation of the Vance Plan on demilitarisation which means that the process of the return of refugees to Western Slavonia could begin. It was not possible to do the same in Eastern Slavonia because there had been no demilitarisation there. You must understand that no one can return to a place where you had armed forces in addition to, and everybody was afraid of that. That is why we asked for those ethnic areas, Serb villages, there shouldn't be any Croatian police officers, only UN personnel. So I'm talking about September 1999, which is a time when realistically it was possible to start the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] excuse me, counsel. We just got in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzakula, there was a mistake but it's been corrected now. Can we now talk about the decision L8 on the return of refugees. The Prosecutor asked you about Article 2 of that decision, and it reads that: "The Secretariat of Interior in charge is required to carry out a background check of the requesting party within 90 days from the day of receipt of the request for return to verify if the individual was (directly or indirectly) involved with any enemy unit or nationalist and fascist party." And if you remember, you replied by saying that this probably meant the ZNG, the Croatian Army and police, the HDZ, and maybe some other parties involved. My impression was that when you said probably, you didn't know exactly to whom this referred, this decision, I mean, and what this directly or indirectly involved in enemy formation meant and which nationalist and fascist parties were they talking about specifically. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there are no specific designations about what forces or parties were involved. That was probably left at the discretion of those who were investigating those issues. But most probably anyone who committed a crime should not return or, rather, should be prosecuted. That was one of the decision passed under the pressure of the international community for the government to adopt a decision on the return, but this was not yet a true democratic decision, because that was April 1992. The conditions were not ripe. But they thought, nevertheless, then if they pass such a decision, that would be sufficient to demonstrate their goodwill to the international community. And as I said, the precondition for the return of refugees is demilitarisation, and this decision was only one in the series of decisions that should change people -- people's state of mind and that things had to change. They still couldn't get over the fact that they had to adopt democratic decisions, because the process of demilitarisation was not yet finished, and any other effort to have people returned would be pointless. How can you return people to an area if you have armed forces walking around the whole territory? Whether they were specifying referring to the ZNG or the HDZ, it was not relevant at that point, but it demonstrated that the government was imposing restrictions. And the same time was done by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people will be prosecuted. The -- the way was not to impose administrative obstacles, and the same was being done by the Croatian authorities. There was no political will, because the authorities didn't want that. Croatia could not face the fact that Croatia would not be an ethnically cleansed state, and the same applied to the Serb territories. And that was the policy that had been pursued for years by Franjo Tudjman, and that could not be overcome overnight. That is why Zecevic spoke as he did. How can one explain that Croats were going to return to Benkovac if those people were expelled from their villages and their houses were ruined? So what was the point of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I totally understand your state of mind, but still the interpreters have to be able to follow you. If they can't, then we'll have a problem with the transcript. So please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I wanted to ask you about this decision which is rather ambiguous, but it does indicate which kind of people would be free to return. I understand your critical views about this decision and the policies pursued in general. At the time, you were deputy prime minister. Why didn't you propose a different wording to this decision and ask for these enemy forces to be specified in more exact terms as well as who these extremists and fascist parties were? That is what I was asking you about, so kindly answer my question.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed the issue of return with the prime minister, and I provided a lot of explanations too. Another time he said, No way. This is not feasible. We are not ready yet. Therefore, what can I do? Even if I made some proposals, and I did speak at sessions that we had to create conditions for the people to return. You can maybe find it in some minutes of the meeting, but believe me, I did address this issue on many occasions, and my views at the government meetings of the RSK were quite clear, because eventually the same person, Mr. Zecevic, because even then in 1991 and 1992, he was a moderate person. What happened to him in the meantime and why he changed, I don't know. If I felt that I wouldn't be able to address this issue with him, I wouldn't have raised it at all. However, having in mind the mind-set of the government at the time, there was no way that any different decision could be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back now to the discussions about the Vance Plan and the meeting of the 9th of December. You were there, as were representatives of the SAO SBWS. I'm going to read out to you only a portion of Ilija Koncarevic's address. You said that he was the president of the Assembly of the SAO SBWS, and that is on page 215. That's P29. Page 215 in Serbo-Croatian and page 58 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Zivanovic needs to approach the microphone. We can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Koncarevic says the following: "I feel like calling you all my brothers right now, and I'll tell you why. "If anyone were to listen to us, it would seem like the Yugoslav Presidency, the dear Bosnian Krajina and Western Slavonia are trying to convince these two Krajinas to accept something. However, gentlemen, we've already agreed to it. "No one among us is any longer considering the option of war. I did not hear anyone during the discussion who wanted to go to war. "Secondly, nobody said that they did not want the UN troops. Mr. Jovic told us that this is the most we can achieve at this moment. But he also said that we will try to exert influence in the drafting of this document to the extent possible in order to have it improved to receive additional guarantees. Could we please discuss that further rather than lamenting on our position. I know that Karadzic and Dzakula wish all the best for me. Hence there is no need for them to try to persuade me any further." Based on what we can see, I'm interested in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, there it is. I'm was waiting for the second -- for the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One would conclude from this that the SBWS accepted the plan along the guidelines of Mr. Jovic pronounced here. He was a member of the Presidency. They wanted to make use of any possibility to have the plan improved and to secure some additional guarantees, if possible. Do you agree with this assertion of mine?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view -- when was this meeting, on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think the 9th.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Vance Plan was not improved and it was not changed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers not overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you this: What would be the point of that meeting, to speak out this way if the Vance Plan had been accepted? It was just a tug-of-war along the lines of, Well, in principle we are for that. Like Babic said, we are in favour of the peace option but provided the forces are deployed here and there at specific locations. Whereas myself and some others were trying to explain that that was possible and acceptable. Had they said clearly, We accept the Vance Plan. Let's move along and implement it, it would have been done differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why does Koncarevic say then that no one said that we do not want any UN forces? This is the maximum that can be achieved at this moment. But he also said that we would try to influence this document to the extent possible, to have it improved and additional assurances received. Could we continue discussing along these lines? So to discuss such proposals in order to receive additional assurances in order to have the document improved, as he put it. The issue was not whether the plan would be accepted. It was clearly said that this was the most that can be achieved at that point in time on the 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Mr. Koncarevic said at the time it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor showed you some footage with Hadzic speaking and Martic and Djukic in attendance. It was when they were promoted to the rank of general. Do you know why they were promoted to the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened immediately after the breakthrough in the corridor area between Banja Luka and Bijeljina; that is to say in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the area of Bosanska Posavina. I think there was a month-long combat there. Following that operation, they were awarded the rank of general for their conduct by the president of the republic, both Martic and -- what was the other person's name? I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention the corridor, can you explain what it was? First of all, where was it located? Second of all, what was its importance?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor was the only passage to the SAO Krajina and that part of Bosanska Krajina around Banja Luka in order to have them linked with Serbia and Belgrade. Around early May, I think, or perhaps June, maybe in mid-May, Croatian forces entered Bosnia and Herzegovina. They crossed the River Sava near Brcko or Plehan, and at the stormed a Serbian village, massacring civilians. The passage, the corridor, was then cut off. A decision was made in Banja Luka and Knin to attempt a breakthrough in order to free up the passage. Apparently there was no medication in the hospitals in Banja Luka, in Knin, and in Bosanska Gradiska. They went ahead with that operation, liberating the area of the corridor. As a consequence, all non-Serbs were driven out of that area, both Croats and Muslims. No one remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The breakthrough, as far as I understood your words, was executed by the army of the SRK, or perhaps the police, and from Republika Srpska, the Serb part of Bosnia. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a joint operation of the two armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the corridor was the only connection between Krajina and Serbia. Was it also the only way to reach Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the only connection between Western Slavonia and Serbia. We could go to Banja Luka and the SAO Krajina even without the corridor, but we could not reach Serbia without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the corridor important in terms of securing humanitarian assistance and secure supplies for the RSK, including Western Slavonia from the then-Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Without that corridor, no humanitarian or any other kind of supplies could come from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a piece of text, an article from "Borba" as well as some footage. It concerns a press conference from September 1991. If you recall that, perhaps I don't need to replay the video. Can you perhaps answer the following question, since you read the text and saw the video: Is it the same press conference, or are those two separate events?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw many things in the past few days. I don't remember exactly which conference you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to assist you concerning the article in "Borba." It refers to borders, stating that borders were being created by force, and it covers a number of questions put to Mr. Hadzic by the journalists present. You commented on a certain portion of the text which has to do with some kind of genetic hatred harboured by some Croats against Serbs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, because we believe that it was the same press conference and that the text is simply a report of the footage. We believe that the text does not, however, reflect faithfully what was truly said at the press conference. That is why I asked you whether you believed it to be one and the same press conference, because it seems that the same things were discussed such as borders, or do you believe it to be two separate events?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have footage on the one hand where we could hear what the president of the republic said. As for the "Borba" article, I understood it as a journalist interpretation of the press conference. Journalists have a certain freedom what to write about. They can skip words. They don't do verbatims. So I don't know whether the journalists copied exactly with a Mr. Hadzic said. The context, however, is identical, the borders, certain issues. So we have the footage, and we have the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I will now show you a document from our list, in English. It is document 2814 in e-court. We haven't received a translation into Serbian. It's a letter drafted by deputy commander of the 5th Military District, Lieutenant-General Andrija Raseta. It has to do with certain crimes or genocide, as he termed it, against the Serb people. I will translate for you the part that we believe to be relevant. It is the second paragraph: [In English] "Starting from November the 1st, 1991, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia have carried out an all-out assault on the territories of West Slavonia and Moslavina. The target" --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apologies. I can barely hear you. The interpretation I'm receiving is very low. Sorry, I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me better now? [In English] "Starting from November the 1st, 1991, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia have carried out an all-out assault on the territories of West Slavonia and Moslavina. The target of this assault are the inhabitants of Serbian nationality who make up the majority of the inhabitants in the wider region of Grubisno Polje. "It has been established beyond dispute that the following villages have been demolished and burned: Velika and Mala Peratovica, Miokovicevo, Veliki and Mali Grdevac, Velika Dapcevica, Sibenik, Gakovo."

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sibenik, Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sibenik, sorry: "According the claims of the refugees, the same fate came to the villages of Velika and Mala Barna, Topolovica, Kovacica, Donja Rasenica, and six others. "In the region of Gakovo, the Croatian armed forces have burnt a forest (630 hectares) in which there were in refugee some -- in refuge some thousand people and it is presumed that they had burnt to death. "Due to danger of genocide, the inhabitants of Serbian nationality from the areas of Moslavina and Western Slavonia have left into refuge. Apart from the refugees in the greater region of Banja Luka, some 4.000, there are around 10.000 more Serbs in refuge on the mountains of Psunj and Papuk, mostly the sick, elderly, women and children. Due to the lack of food and medicaments and extremely cold weather, these people are in a very critical position." [Interpretation] I think this suffices. I won't read it to the end. Does this accurately reflect the situation you testified to about the operation in November 1991 in Grubisno Polje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you clarify? This is a letter from whom to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It is a letter of deputy commander Lieutenant-Colonel General Andrija Raseta, deputy commander of JNA, to the command of the 5th Army district of JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was sent to the head of the EC monitor mission for Yugoslavia in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text that you have translated for me is accurate save for the 630 hectares and several thousand people, which is incorrect. That was an expectation until the refugees actually emerged. As for the 10.000 at Psunj and Papuk, that is not correct. There was over 25.000 refugees. There was a large concentration of Serbs who fled the nearby towns and were located in these villages, and as they were withdrawing from these villages, primarily Grubisno Polje, there was torching, explosives were laid, and the remaining civilians were killed. That much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will tender this document into evidence. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects, Mr. President. We've heard a lot of evidence and testimony from the witness, and rightfully so, about the incidents, the crimes against Serb populations in Western Slavonia. We haven't objected because it does relate to relevant context, but the Prosecution's position is that we're moving across now into tu quoque. It's not clearly precisely what this document adds to what the witness -- and by the way, the witness has indicated that significant portions of this are not correct, but it's not clear what the document adds beyond tu quoque on top of the context that has been fully developed during the cross-examination. So the Prosecution is going to start objecting -- raising objections on the grounds of tu quoque such as to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We do not have tu quoque defence. We do not tender this document to prove that the acts or the conduct of the accused are justified with such -- such acts of the opposing side. It just should corroborate the witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the possibility of sliding into tu quoque apart, isn't this document of assistance inasmuch as it being addressed to the head of the EC monitor mission memorialises a particular concern that a relevant party had?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes - excuse me - yes, Your Honour. It does memorialise a concern that this JNA officer had, but the concern that he's expressing is, in our respectful submission -- doesn't add anything to the testimony given by the witness, and really in terms of the purpose of its being tendered into evidence can only really go to tu quoque, because, again, in terms of the -- the events, the concerns, the crimes being committed against Serb populations, there is ample evidence now, and it's come in without objection. It just seemed to the Prosecution, Your Honour, that we're crossing the line now and just going into gratuitous, if you will, tu quoque and it doesn't add anything to what we've already got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Admit and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2814 shall be assigned Exhibit D3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I will show you another very short document. It's 65 ter 1428. It's a letter. Cyrus Vance sent it to President Milosevic on the 22nd of January, 1993, Witness. Tudjman -- this document is being translated as well. It is very short, and I will read it out for you: [In English] "I must talk to you immediately. As you know, fighting has broken out between Tudjman's people and armed forces in the area of Maslenica. About an hour ago, Tudjman committed to me that he had given the order to stop fighting. It is urgent that you and I talk about how to get word to the other side to stop fighting. "Please call me immediately." [Interpretation] You testified, among other things, about various Croatian operations, including Operation Maslenica. Based on your evidence, it followed that the operations came about because the Republic of the Serbian Krajina had not been demilitarised and that this was the reason that led to these operations.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have difficulty hearing you. You should speak to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that the operations such as the Miljevac Plateau, Medak pocket, Maslenica, were brought about by the fact that the Republic of the Serbian Krajina had not been demilitarised. Hence my question: Nowhere in this letter did I observe that Tudjman or anyone else justified the operations by the Croatian forces by the fact that the RSK had not been demilitarised. Quite the contrary. Tudjman issued the order that the filing between the Croatian and Serbian forces should cease. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've obviously failed to understand my yesterday's testimony concerning the Miljevac Plateau, Maslenica, and Medak pocket. You can see that this letter, too, refers to a war between Tudjman's forces and other forces - I suppose, I don't see the translation - that there were two armed forces clashing. I spoke of these incidents in these terms. The UN forces that were present there did not get involved in the protection of the area when the Croatian Army or the police, I think it was the army, launched an attack on the Miljevac Plateau and Maslenica and, let me add, the Medak pocket. Because of the fact that the UN forces did not want to constitute a buffer zone between two armies, that's why I emphasised the issue of demilitarisation. And I said that had the area been demilitarised, the UN forces would have had an obligation to defend the area which would have averted a conflict between the Croatian Army and the Serbian Army, because we are talking about two armed forces clashing. In other words, I did not say as you termed it now that the fact that the area had not been demilitarised, that moved the Croatian forces to react and attack. No, it is the issue of the fact that the Croatian forces fought the Serbian forces simply because the UN forces did not intervene and assume the duty of defending the area. Have you understood me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have. However, based on my observation of this text, Tudjman ordered that all these operations be brought to a stop exactly because the areas were under the protection of the UN forces, quite apart from the fact that there was some other armed force present there as well.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not justifying Tudjman's operations at all. I condemn them. This was area under protection, but the UN did not take upon themselves in military terms the obligation to defend the area, because the area had not been demilitarised. And this led to the two armies clashing. I do condemn the fact that Tudjman launched this action and this was an area -- Maslenica was not used for several years to come. Had the area however been demilitarised, it would have been the obligation of UN soldiers to guard the area. It turned out, and I said so, that the army of Republic of Serbian Krajina which was at Maslenica did not have the force to defend the area. So what was the point of demilitarisation then? We had an army that was unable to defend it, and had the UN assumed their obligations, they would have defended the area, and Tudjman would have been accused of having attacked the UN forces. This was the context of my words, so please view them within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, we have certain information concerning the action directed toward Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 5868. It should not be presented at the screen, and relevant paragraphs are 49 to 61. It is on the list, 21st item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivanovic, they are telling me that you should switch both of your microphones on as you keep moving and they can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, we have information, and I cannot give you the sources under the rules before the Tribunal. We have information about the action launched at Pakrac, and based on the information we have, the action had been pre-planned by the Serbian side, and based on the information we have, you took part in the planning of the action. Since the version of the events you related was different, can you tell us if the information we have is correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What sort of plan is this? What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the action against Pakrac which you said was carried out on the 1st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't lead the action, but I was present there. It was led by the police chief who, on the orders of the president of the Municipal Assembly and the president of the Executive Board, was told in writing to disarm the active duty corps of the newly arrived Croatian police and to call up the reserve police force. In response, a special Croatian police unit was sent to the Pakrac area to capture the Pakrac police station. I don't see how I was able to take part in this action since it was undertaken by the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, and if -- on the other side it was arranged by the chief of police on the orders of these two individuals. So I don't see how I could have taken any part in that context. I was present there, and I was present in the negotiations after the action concerning demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not take part in the preparations either?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't have any powers that would enable me to make any plans. Nobody expected Croatia to send Special Police forces against the Pakrac police, and -- and had the newly arrived Croatian police not taken out of the police station the long-barrelled weapons and had this not been seen by the local policemen who reported it to the chief of police, this would not have happened. Otherwise, it would have been impossible for me to persuade anyone to sign anything. These are mere imputations against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, we are nearing the end of your cross-examination. The last topic I wanted to discuss with you was the Daruvar Agreement. You testified about it here. We know what it was about. When you were deputy prime minister of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, did you inform the government of the ongoing negotiations with the Croatian side and that such an agreement would be stipulated?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not inform the government, and I will tell you why I didn't do so. If several days earlier Mr. Hadzic had ordered the commander of the RSK army that we in Western Slavonia should take out the heavy weaponry and tanks out of the warehouses and attack Novska and Nova Gradiska where civilians lived, thereby engaging us in a war without any reason in an area that was demilitarised - let me stress this again - we were being pushed into committing a crime so that we would come in harm's way. We ourselves did not want to get involved in any such conflicts, but then we had to commit to writing our obligation that we would be considered responsible if the Croatian forces attacked the area because we refused to take out heavy weaponry. At that point we realised that we had to wage our own policy so that our area would not fare the way Maslenica and Medak Pocket fared. If Goran Hadzic took upon himself the right to command from Belgrade the RSK commander that we should attack these place - and he couldn't know what the situation was like there, we knew that there was no danger - that meant that we had to take things into our own hands. We had to take charge of things. We saw that they wanted to create an equilibrium. If the Croatians attacked Maslenica, let us open up a front at this end. But this wasn't about opening up fronts. It was about the peace process. However, I didn't have any like-minded people. But we had the Assembly of Western Slavonia which meant that we had the ride to negotiate, we had the right to sign documents, and we had the right to present this before the Assembly. We had that right, and we had that legitimacy. And that was the reason that prompted me to act as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, it would have been only natural for you to have informed them of it. Our case is that there was no order coming from Hadzic of that sort. But let me tell you something else: In that event, if you wanted to wage your own policy, would it not have been logical for you to have told the government members that you no longer wanted to have any part in this and that you wanted to pursue a separate policy quite apart from the policy of the RSK and that you would be entering into negotiations with the Croatian side independently?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we been able to say as much without incurring any consequences, we would have. However, it turned out that the consequences were grave. They would not allow you the right to take charge of your own life and freedom. That right was only granted to them to take decisions when and how they wished. We didn't have an interlocutor, and there were lives at stake. You have to understand, 600 children 100 metres from the separation line, and these children were aged up to 15 years of age, and somebody wanted to play war. Come on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have a clarification to ask. Mr. Dzakula, you say, "They would not allow you the right to take charge of your own life and freedom. We didn't have ..." Now, I mean "they." Who do you mean by "they"? "They would not allow you the right."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I mean the Krajina authorities, Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Martic, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's another thing I'm interested in, Mr. Dzakula. You said that you did not inform them of this because you didn't want to incur any consequences. I suppose that you knew that if you concluded the agreement, consequences would be forthcoming. So I can't understand this. I suppose you could have incurred consequences that would not have been as grave had you informed them of your dealings rather than allow them to hear of it themselves?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they heard of it indirectly. It did not come as a surprise. As for consequences, well, they did not dare to incur -- to impose any, because the Assembly was the legitimate organ above Mr. Hadzic or Mr. Martic. In this case, they did not have the jurisdiction that was necessary. But it turned out that arresting people came easy to them, and it turned out also that killing people came easy to them, and I thought that I would be protected by the United Nations from the terror that they inflicted upon those of us who wanted to preserve peace and freedom in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. This concludes my cross-examination. [In English] Sorry, I will use the break. Maybe we shall have -- maybe we will have some more questions. I think that we -- that some time was left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was just going to say that that's the perfect timing, Mr. Zivanovic, but it still is. So we take the break, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will return at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have anything further in cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just confront the witness with a document. I tried to do that yesterday, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- for some technical reason I didn't manage to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I will ask you only one question that I attempted to put to you yesterday, but I had some technical problems with that. Let us look at your statement, which is 65 ter 5595. It's number 12 in our list. Page 13 in English. We need two penultimate lines. In B/C/S, it's page 15, the first two paragraphs. I'm going to read to you, because it's very short, and you say: "As I already said, on the 26th of February, 1992, the SAO Slavonia joined the SAO Krajina and the SAO Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem in order to form the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We in Western Slavonia heard that the Sarajevo agreement was signed on the 2nd of January, 1992, and that the Vance Peace Plan was accepted. As the situation in Slavonia was very chaotic, a few of us who were representatives of the civilian authorities of the SAO Western Slavonia, namely Dusan Ecimovic, Veljko Vukic, Obrad Ivanovic, Milenko Miletic and several others, were interested in implementing the Vance Plan. Our position did not allow us to play a solo game and we saw that the Yugoslav policies was in --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Yugoslavia policy was in favour of the peace plan." [In English] It is further on, page 14 of the English, just to ... [Interpretation] "In addition, we heard that Milan Babic would not be allowed to be the leading political figure in the region, which was an additional reason to decide and realise that it is in our interest to join our forces and implement the Vance Peace Plan. The only objection that we had was that Podravska Slatina was not included in the territories covered by the peace plan. The idea that Hadzic would be president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina encouraged us as he was in favour of the plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember this statement of yours, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that written statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The inference that one can draw from this statement is that one of the reasons, the motives for your joining the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I'm talking about Western Slavonia, was the fact that Milan Babic was no longer to be the leading political figure and that you were encouraged by the fact that Goran Hadzic, who was in favour of the peace plan, was to become the president.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't find anywhere in our statement that you said that Hadzic was against the plan.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't against the plan, but later on he failed to implement it. I made mention of this major meeting of the Presidency, and at the end I said that Goran Hadzic was in favour of the Vance Plan. However, at a later stage when the government was formed, they, including Hadzic, did not implement the plan to the full, but believe me, it would have been better for all of us if they had done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the constitution of the RSK provides that the policy in the RSK is to be implemented by the government and not the president. Would you agree with me with that? I think it's Article 84 of the constitution, and the document is L3.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what the constitution stipulates, but it also stipulates all the duties of the president of the republic are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before redirect, we would like to rule on Mr. Zivanovic's objection and Mr. Stringer's request regarding the new documents to be used in redirect, documents we understand that are on the 65 ter list. We don't think that Mr. Zivanovic's objection is justified, and his objection therefore is overruled and the documents may be used insofar they are used to redirect and to address issues that came out of cross-examination, of course. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do not have too much, I don't think, in terms of redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, hopefully we'll be done in half an hour or so. The first item, actually, is one of the last ones that counsel just took you to. He showed you a part of your OTP witness statement from May of 2002, and he read to you the passage about the proposal on the Vance Plan, and I had wanted to come back to this as well. Page 478 from yesterday's transcript, at the bottom, counsel asked you, Mr. Dzakula, about whether the Vance Plan was -- was signed or agreed on the 2nd of December or the 2nd of January. I should say 2nd of December, 1991, or the 2nd of January, 1992. And at the time you testified yesterday, Mr. Dzakula, you indicated that you weren't -- you couldn't recall for sure whether it was the 2nd of December or the 2nd of January. Do you remember that? You were referring to the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I may, I'll take you back briefly and quickly to the same passage that counsel just read to you which in your witness statement you said: "We in Western Slavonia heard that the Sarajevo Agreement was signed on 2 January, the 2nd of January, 1992, and that the Vance Peace Plan was accepted." So my question, Mr. Dzakula, is simply whether that refreshes your recollection, that it was in fact on the 2nd of January when the Sarajevo Agreement was signed that you had referred to.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we discussed the Vance Plan in -- during December, and I still think that it was on the 2nd of December, although the statement says that it's the 2nd of January. However, if this date is officially known, I don't know why you're asking me to remember that. Everybody knows when this document was signed. So I'm a bit confused. I know that we debated it on the 9th and the 12th of December, so if we already discussed it, it just tells me that it had already been accepted, and we continued our discussion throughout January. I still think that that was the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to clarify one part of your testimony from yesterday, which is at page 480 of the transcript. You were talking again about the Vance Plan, and you were asked: "When did you learn for the first time that Goran Hadzic was against the plan?" And then this is 470, line -- 479, line 22. And then, Mr. Dzakula, you said that Mr. Hadzic had attended one session, one SFRY Presidency session. He did not attend another. And then skipping over, you said: "I don't want to repeat the entire minutes, but later on as it turned out, Mr. Hadzic accepted the Vance Plan, and he backed it up." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In English they gave us the words "he backed it up," and I wanted to ask you to clarify that, because it could be that someone reading the transcript concludes that Mr. Hadzic accepted the plan and that he fully supported it or implemented it, and I want to ask you whether that is a correct interpretation of your answer here, that he backed it up.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Hadzic, one can say positively, publicly accepted in mid-January, that is when Hadzic and Dzakula accepted it, but Babic didn't. He said that he was favour at this important meeting that we kept coming back, but you heard a minute ago that on the 12th of December, Koncarevic and I were trying to persuade the people of Western Slavonia with regard to accept the Vance Plan. If it had been accepted, there wouldn't be such a long debate. As I said, it was just a declaratory statement of acceptance, but later on it was not implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were the provisions on demilitarisation implemented by the RSK side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The provisions on demilitarisation were not implemented in either SBWS or in the Krajina. The only area where it was implemented was Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again in terms of Mr. Hadzic's acceptance of the plan, did Mr. Hadzic accept demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Hadzic did not accept demilitarisation, because it was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you've been asked a couple times this morning, there was one passage at page 5 of today's transcript in which a distinction was drawn between RSK government policy or an administrative position of the RSK government in respect of refugees. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question from my learned friend was that -- he said: "In other words, what prevented the return of Serbs to Western Slavonia was purely administrative. In other words, it was based on the decision of the RSK government and perhaps the government of Croatia." And you answered: "Yes." Now, my question is this: Goran Hadzic, the individual, the man Goran Hadzic, if you know, what was his position on the question of return both of Serbs to Western Slavonia as well as Croats to places such as Ilok in the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Hadzic was not in favour of the return of Croats to Eastern Slavonia because he always linked it with the return of Serbs to Western Slavonia, and he indicated that the conditions were not yet ripe for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was the first condition that had to be overcome?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and the most important precondition was demilitarisation. You cannot start the return of refugees before the UN took over the responsibility for the protection and only demilitarisation was carried through and only after that could the refugees return to Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, we looked at -- you were shown a video first by the Prosecution and then by the Defence during your cross-examination, and you were asked questions about whether it was a meeting in Beli Manastir or Borovo Selo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we would like to show you a different video, and we'll play it now and you can watch and listen, and tell us whether this, whether you have any comments about this video, the location and the events taking place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please give a 65 ter reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My apologies. 65 ter reference is 4842.1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Anchor: The session of all three Assemblies of Serbian region ended last night in Borovo Selo. All 236 MPs who attended the session showed notably high level of unity. Djordje Gajdosevic reports: "Reporter: The new president of the Republic of Krajina, Goran Hadzic, who stated he was taking this position wishing only to contribute to the unity of Serbian people. All present expressed their hope to the coming multi-party elections where new capable people would surface, would contribute to this. New amendments, especially the ones referring to the term autonomous region were mostly discussed. Any mention of the word autonomy strikes fear of Croatian authorities returning to these territories, so it was said at the end that the Republic of Srpska Krajina was made up of Serbian regions. The entire session proceeded in desire to avoid schism within Serbian people. A communique signed by the president Mile Paspalj called on unit of Serbian people and urged the Serbs not to take part at a rally scheduled for 9th March in Belgrade and other places. Only a couple of years ago, the communique reads Serbian people believed that times when every event was history and every date reminder of significant historical mistakes were gone for ever. This is how it was in Borovo Selo yesterday, the place that a year ago made it clear to secessionists that Serbian people in these territories recognise only Serbian and Yugoslav laws. Similar things were said at yesterday's session as well, proof that these are people who are true to themselves. "Anchor: We hereby send our best wishes for success with your work --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, now having seen this video footage, does it affect in any way your testimony about the meetings, the February 1992 meeting, 26th of February, whether the various video footages, any of them, correspond to that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This footage has reminded me that the Assembly was held in Borovo Selo and that the RSK was established there on the 26th of February, and it fully corresponds to the events of that day. By looking at this footage and the people present there refreshed my memory entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please pull up Exhibit P42. And this relates -- I'm looking at page 516 of yesterday's transcript, at the bottom of -- you were talking about your efforts and dealings with Mr. Goulding on the refugee issues in Western Slavonia, and counsel made a reference to your position in the RSK government as being involved in forestry, and I just wanted to come back to that, because to clarify, your dealings with the UN and your involved in refugee issues for Western Slavonia, was that beyond your remit as a minister or vice-president of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not go beyond my authorities, because you will remember that together with Mr. Zdravko Zecevic, the prime minister of the RSK, I went to New York to discuss the Vance Plan. So if I was authorised at that time and if there was a need that I join the prime minister and the minister of defence for me to go to New York and discuss the importance of the Vance Plan and everything else, then I think that I had every right, that all the activities that I was involved and advocated in New York, I should do the same in Western Slavonia. The UN always made references to my name as well, and this is a confirmation, this trip, of how important my role was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in P42, we can come back to it if you need to look at it, but you refer to a visitation programme. I should say not you, but Mr. Nambiar who is writing this document refers to a visitation programme. Could you just very briefly describe what is the programme. In terms of your dealing with the UN people, were you hiding this from the RSK authorities? Was this something that you were concealing, or was this something that you were doing openly?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was openly involved in these activities. It could not have been implemented without the knowledge of the local police that was directly under the command of Mr. Martic, the minister of police in Knin. These visits were of such nature that Serbs wanted to go to their villages alongside UN forces and only after that would they decide whether to return. We mentioned this check-point where people used to meet and discuss these issues. All of that was done with the approval and blessing of the police, and that could not have been done without the knowledge of the minister, because that was such a critical issue. So nothing was done in secrecy. Everybody was quite aware of every move that we made, including the eventual signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's indicated in this document, but did the visitation programme enjoy the support of the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not opposed, but they were not impressed with our move either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Today, Mr. Dzakula, you were shown Exhibit 65 ter 5516.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could just put that back up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, should we use this document in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Oh, apologies. Yes, if we could please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you were asked earlier today about your knowledge of an operation to take the region of the Bosanska Posavina or the Posavina corridor in summer of 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you said this was a joint military operation. And I just wanted to clarify, who were the armed forces on the Serb side that participated jointly in this operation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police force of the RSK headed by Mr. Martic and the Banja Luka Corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, the -- the VRS, and the references in the transcript on this, to Banja Luka, those are all based in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They were in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on page 18 of today's transcript, line 3, Mr. Dzakula, you said on this that: "A decision was made in Banja Luka and Knin to attempt a breakthrough in order to free up the passage." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' permission, I'd like to show one video-clip that relates to this issue. It is 65 ter 4945.2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have the time reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The time reference is 41 minutes, 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Milan Martic: Before I say anything, let us hold a minute of silence in honour of all our killed soldiers, the Serbian heroes who fell at this corridor and the soldiers who fell at the Miljevacka Plateau. May they rest in peace. "All: May they rest in peace. "Milan Martic: Dear fellow citizens, let me thank you first for your magnificent welcome. I know these are not the times of celebrations, because we are living in a very unfortunate times. Trouble and misfortune forced us to follow this path. You were all witnesses when we were closed off and attacked, when all roads towards the Republic of Srpska Krajina were closed off and when it was made impossible for us to have the most basic means of living, no medicine, our sick were dying, our wives were forced to ask foreign soldiers for cigarettes. We suffered the ultimate misfortune. We addressed our requests to UNPROFOR to make that passage and corridor available to us. But UNPROFOR did not meet that request and made that passage available. This should not be a surprise when it is known that the US, Germany, and other countries which most certainly are not well-intentioned toward the Serbian people are directing UNPROFOR. All credit to the Kenyans who are definitely for us, but the majority ... but the majority of the representatives of UNPROFOR are most certainly not well-intentioned towards us and do not have our best interest at heart and that is why we decided not to beg anyone for mercy, not even UNPROFOR, not Genscher, not Kohl, not Bush, and not that wretched Yeltsin. We had set off to penetrate the corridor with our Serbian heroes, aware that it could cost us our lives. Unfortunately, it did indeed happen. And 25 of our heroes from the Krajina police brigade died in that bloody battle for the corridor. Those men were certainly not killed or to be erased from our memory. Those are the Serbian Obilics, rest assured. Commander Raso, one of the biggest heroes ever known to the Serbian people, will go down in history of the Serbian people and that is where he belongs. All others who fell in glory at that corridor, in order to secure a better future for you, deserve that place. They were also not killed in vain, and it is up to us who stayed behind not to forget their families and we will never do that. We will never forget them, rest assured. I am confident that when we had set off we had a blessing of 99 per cent of you, and that you were convinced that we would complete our task assigned to us by our president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mr. Goran Hadzic, and by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to open up this corridor. You were convinced that we would complete the task. You knew that these heroes, who participated in many battles, and had never lost a battle nor would they lose the battle with Ustashas and their scum, the Green Berets. I thank you for that from my heart, for the trust, and after all, I say: 'We completed our task.' On a number of occasions, we sent messages about the heroic combat of our men, fighting hand -- side by side with the enemy and leaving the trace, and they lived up to the famous image of the 'Knindzas' soldiers at the front line. But we will also not forgive those pathetic ones who were hoping for our return in caskets, that our action would fail, and they are punished enough by their thinking alone and they should not be judged. And this whole situation, this bloody combat for our better future, we must give our thanks to all the soldiers who took part in that heroic battle. That is to say, the soldiers of the Republic of Serbian Krajina led by General Momir Talic and all his troops, and the fighters who joined us on arrival in Banja Luka, Prnjavor, Doboj. We were met there with such enthusiasm by the people since we knew -- they knew we were coming with good intentions, to penetrate the corridor. They were in a situation similar to ours. At that place, in this combat, I think the Serbian unit had never shone so bright as now, a brother giving life for a brother. That can only be seen at the corridor and nowhere else. The corridor which was over 120 kilometres in length at the front line, it had been mopped up for us for the full 38 days. We said we would not come back until we achieved the final victory, until we forced the enemy across the Sava. Our task was to push them back across the Sava River, and we succeeded."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I know it's lengthy, Your Honours. I apologise. I thought for completeness, we could play the entire transcript. We're reaching the end, but we have already covered the point I wanted to raise with Mr. Dzakula, so I'm in your hands. We can play the remainder or if Your Honours wish to move to the main point, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We would prefer you move to the main point, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, going back to your testimony from today where you said a decision -- well, first of all, let me ask, this speech that we've just seen part of, do you know what this relates to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to a celebration held upon the breakthrough of the corridor, and the two generals were promoted that day by the president of the republic, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you just said promoted by President Hadzic. Do you know if this video relates to an earlier video shown during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have shown me when we discussed their promotions by Goran Hadzic, I think it was the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
